overview.title: Broadcasting: a worked example and a naive implementation
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.section: 2.3 The gears of neural networks: Tensor operations
overview.main_topic: How a smaller tensor is virtually expanded (broadcast) to match a larger one so that element-wise operations can be applied, illustrated with a (32, 10) matrix and a (10,) vector.
overview.central_idea: Broadcasting adds axes to the smaller tensor and then (virtually) repeats it along those axes until both tensors have the same shape; NumPy performs this repetition at the algorithmic level without allocating a new tensor.
overview.importance: Every `Dense` layer computes `W @ x + b`, where `b` is a vector added to a matrix. Understanding broadcasting explains how that addition is legal and efficient, and it is the key to reading almost any NumPy/Keras shape error you will ever meet.
learning_objectives: Describe the two steps of broadcasting (adding axes, then repeating along them).
Explain why the repetition is virtual and why that matters for memory.
Trace the naive matrix-plus-vector loop and relate it to the broadcast rule.
State the general shape-compatibility rule for broadcasting given on this page.
prerequisites: Element-wise operations and the naive `naive_add` implementation (p.53)
The Dense layer formula `output = relu(dot(input, W) + b)` (p.52)

summary:
This page completes the explanation of **broadcasting** begun on p.54. The second step of broadcasting is stated first: after new (broadcast) axes have been added to the smaller tensor, that tensor is *repeated* along the new axes until its shape matches the larger tensor.

The authors then walk through a concrete example. `X` is a random matrix of shape `(32, 10)` and `y` a random vector of shape `(10,)`. Step one: `y = np.expand_dims(y, axis=0)` inserts an empty first axis so that `y` has shape `(1, 10)`. Step two: `Y = np.tile(y, (32, 1))` repeats `y` 32 times along axis 0, producing `Y` with shape `(32, 10)` and the property that every row `Y[i, :]` equals the original `y`. Now `X` and `Y` have identical shapes, so the element-wise addition from p.53 applies directly.

A crucial implementation remark follows: no new rank-2 tensor is ever materialised when NumPy broadcasts, because that would be "terribly inefficient". The repetition is **entirely virtual** — it happens at the algorithmic level, not at the memory level. The mental model of a vector copied 32 times is nonetheless useful. To make the algorithm explicit the page shows `naive_add_matrix_and_vector(x, y)`: it asserts that `x` is rank 2, `y` is rank 1, and that `x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]`; it copies `x` to avoid overwriting the input; then two nested loops add `y[j]` to every element `x[i, j]`. The vector index depends only on the column `j`, which is exactly what "repeat along axis 0" means.

Finally the page states the general rule: an element-wise operation between a tensor of shape `(a, b, … n, n + 1, … m)` and one of shape `(n, n + 1, … m)` is permitted, with broadcasting happening automatically over axes `a` through `n − 1` — i.e. the smaller tensor's shape must match the *trailing* axes of the larger one.

paragraphs.excerpt: The smaller tensor is repeated alongside these new axes to match the full shape
paragraphs.what_it_says: This is the second bullet of the two-step description of broadcasting started on p.54: once broadcast axes have been added to the smaller tensor, it is repeated along those axes until its shape equals the shape of the larger tensor.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Step one (p.54) fixes the *rank* mismatch by inserting axes of size 1; step two fixes the *size* mismatch along those axes by copying the data. After both steps the two operands have the same shape, so the ordinary element-wise rules from p.53 apply.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the conceptual contract behind `W @ x + b` in a `Dense` layer: `b` is a vector, the product is a matrix, and the addition only makes sense because `b` is treated as if it were copied once per sample.

terminology.meaning: The new axes (of length 1) inserted into the smaller tensor so that its `ndim` matches the larger tensor's (named on p.54).

connections: p.54: the first bullet — adding broadcast axes to match `ndim`.
p.53: element-wise operations require operands of the same shape.

paragraphs.excerpt: Let’s look at a concrete example. Consider X with shape (32, 10) and y
paragraphs.what_it_says: The authors set up a concrete case: a matrix `X` of shape `(32, 10)` and a vector `y` of shape `(10,)`, created with `np.random.random`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The numbers are chosen to look like a mini-batch: 32 samples, each a 10-dimensional feature vector (compare the batch-axis convention on p.49). The vector `y` has one entry per feature, exactly like a bias vector in a `Dense` layer with 10 units.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: A fixed, small example lets you check every shape by hand; the same reasoning scales to `(128, 512) + (512,)` or larger.

terminology.meaning: A rank-1 tensor (vector) with 10 entries; the trailing comma marks a one-element tuple (p.47).

connections: p.49: the first axis of a data tensor is the batch/samples axis.
p.47: shape is a tuple of per-axis sizes.

paragraphs.excerpt: First, we add an empty first axis to y, whose shape becomes (1, 10):
paragraphs.what_it_says: Step one is done with `np.expand_dims(y, axis=0)`: a new axis of length 1 is inserted in front, so `y` becomes `(1, 10)`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: `y` now has `ndim == 2`, the same rank as `X`, but still holds the same 10 numbers — the new axis is 'empty' in the sense that it carries no additional data.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Matching rank is the precondition for the repeat step; a `(1, 10)` tensor is a one-row matrix, so it can be stacked row-wise.
paragraphs.technical_idea: `axis=0` puts the new axis first; `np.expand_dims(y, axis=1)` would have produced `(10, 1)`, a column, which would broadcast against a `(10, k)` matrix instead.

terminology.meaning: NumPy function that inserts a new axis of size 1 at the given position without changing the data.

connections: p.47: `ndim` is the number of axes.

paragraphs.excerpt: Then, we repeat y 32 times alongside this new axis, so that we end
paragraphs.what_it_says: Step two uses `np.tile(y, (32, 1))` to repeat `y` 32 times along axis 0 and once along axis 1, giving `Y` of shape `(32, 10)` such that `Y[i, :] == y` for every `i` in `range(0, 32)`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: `Y` is a matrix whose 32 rows are all identical copies of the original vector. The tuple `(32, 1)` passed to `tile` gives the repeat count per axis.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: After this step `X` and `Y` have the same shape and can be added element-wise; this is the explicit (materialised) version of what broadcasting does implicitly.
paragraphs.technical_idea: `Y[i, :]` selects row `i` using the slicing syntax introduced on p.49.

terminology.meaning: NumPy function that builds a larger array by repeating the input a given number of times along each axis.

connections: p.53: element-wise addition of same-shape tensors.

paragraphs.excerpt: At this point, we can add X and Y because they have the same shape.
paragraphs.what_it_says: With both tensors at shape `(32, 10)`, ordinary element-wise addition applies.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The whole purpose of the two steps was to reduce the mixed-shape case to the same-shape case already covered by `naive_add` on p.53.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows that broadcasting is not a new kind of operation, just a shape-preparation step in front of an element-wise one.

paragraphs.excerpt: In terms of implementation, no new rank-2 tensor is created because that would
paragraphs.what_it_says: In a real implementation the repeated tensor `Y` is never built — that would be terribly inefficient. The repetition is entirely virtual, happening at the algorithmic level rather than the memory level. Still, imagining the vector copied 32 times along a new axis is a useful mental model, and the authors introduce a naive implementation to show the algorithm.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The `np.tile` call above was pedagogical. NumPy's `X + y` instead loops in a way that reads `y[j]` for every row, so the memory cost stays at `10` numbers rather than `32 × 10`. For a batch of 1,000,000 samples and a 512-unit layer the difference is a 512-float vector versus a 2 GB matrix.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This distinction is why broadcasting is free in practice and why you should write `X + y` rather than `X + np.tile(...)` in your own code.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: NumPy implements the virtual repeat with a zero-stride view — the broadcast axis has stride 0, so every index along it maps to the same memory address.

terminology.meaning: Treating a tensor as if it were copied along an axis, without actually storing the copies.

connections: p.54: vectorised NumPy operations are implemented in C/Fortran for speed.

paragraphs.excerpt: With broadcasting, you can generally apply two-tensor element-wise operations if one
paragraphs.what_it_says: The general rule: if one tensor has shape `(a, b, … n, n + 1, … m)` and the other has shape `(n, n + 1, … m)`, an element-wise operation is allowed, and broadcasting happens automatically over axes `a` through `n − 1`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The smaller tensor's shape must equal the *trailing* part of the larger tensor's shape. The leading axes of the larger tensor are the ones along which the smaller tensor is virtually repeated. In the example, `(32, 10)` versus `(10,)`: the trailing `10` matches and broadcasting occurs over the single leading axis of size 32.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This rule lets you predict whether an operation such as `(64, 28, 28, 3) * (3,)` (scaling each colour channel) is valid — it is — and whether `(32, 10) + (32,)` is valid — it is not, because `32 ≠ 10` on the trailing axis.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: NumPy's full rule is slightly more general — axes of size 1 in either tensor are also stretched — but the trailing-axes rule stated here covers the vast majority of deep-learning uses.

terminology.meaning: The last axes of a shape tuple; broadcasting compares shapes from the right.

connections: p.56: the next page applies `np.maximum` to tensors of different shapes via this rule.

concepts.name: Broadcasting
concepts.definition: The automatic expansion of a smaller tensor — by adding axes and virtually repeating it along them — so that an element-wise operation can be applied with a larger tensor of compatible shape.
concepts.intuition: Adding a vector to every row of a matrix is like adding the same bias to every sample in a batch; you do not need 32 copies of the bias, just the rule 'use the same one each time'.
concepts.technical: Two steps: (1) insert broadcast axes of size 1 so the ranks match; (2) repeat along them. Allowed when the smaller shape `(n, …, m)` equals the trailing axes of the larger shape `(a, …, n, …, m)`; broadcasting occurs over axes `a` through `n − 1`. The repetition is virtual (no new tensor is allocated).
concepts.significance: It is how `W @ x + b` in a `Dense` layer works and how most per-feature scaling/normalisation is written in NumPy and Keras.
concepts.example: `X` of shape `(32, 10)` plus `y` of shape `(10,)`: `y` → `(1, 10)` → virtually `(32, 10)`; result `X[i, j] + y[j]`.
concepts.misconception: That broadcasting physically creates the enlarged tensor. It does not; `np.tile` on this page is only a teaching device.

concepts.name: Element-wise operation
concepts.definition: An operation applied independently to each entry of a tensor (or to each pair of corresponding entries of two same-shape tensors).
concepts.intuition: Think of it as the same tiny calculation run once per cell, with no cell depending on any other.
concepts.technical: For addition, `z[i, j] = x[i, j] + y[i, j]`; such loops are embarrassingly parallel and are executed by vectorised C/Fortran kernels (p.54). Broadcasting extends them to operands whose shapes differ but are compatible.
concepts.significance: Activations (`relu`) and biases in neural networks are element-wise; they form half of what a `Dense` layer does.
concepts.example: `naive_add_matrix_and_vector` is an element-wise addition where the second operand is indexed only by `j`.
concepts.misconception: That `+` on two tensors of different shapes is an error; it is fine whenever broadcasting applies.

concepts.name: Tensor shape and rank
concepts.definition: The shape is the tuple of sizes along each axis; the rank (`ndim`) is the number of axes.
concepts.intuition: Shape tells you how big the box is in each direction; rank tells you how many directions there are.
concepts.technical: `np.expand_dims` changes the rank without changing the data; `np.tile` changes sizes along axes by copying data. `len(x.shape)` equals `x.ndim`.
concepts.significance: Every broadcasting decision is made purely from shapes, which is why the naive function asserts on `len(x.shape)` and `x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]`.
concepts.example: `(10,)` has rank 1; `(1, 10)` has rank 2 and the same 10 numbers.
concepts.misconception: That `(10,)` and `(1, 10)` are the same tensor; they hold the same data but have different ranks, which matters for which axis gets broadcast.

math.title: Matrix-plus-vector addition via broadcasting
math.source_text: x[i, j] += y[j]  (inside the nested loops of naive_add_matrix_and_vector)

variables.meaning: The larger tensor, a matrix of shape (32, 10).
The smaller tensor, a vector of shape (10,).
The result, a matrix of shape (32, 10).
Row (sample) index — the broadcast axis; y does not depend on it.
Column (feature) index — the axis shared by X and y.

math.operations: For every row i and column j, add the j-th entry of y to the (i, j) entry of X. Because y is indexed only by j, every row receives the same vector.
math.purpose: This is the precise meaning of 'repeat y along axis 0 and add'. It is also exactly the `+ b` in a Dense layer, where each sample in the batch gets the same bias.
math.interpretation: Equivalent to X + Y where Y = tile(expand_dims(y, 0), (32, 1)), but without ever storing Y.
math.intuition: Picture the vector y lying under the matrix; slide it along to each row and add.
math.numerical_example:
Take a 2×3 case instead of 32×10 (same rule):

$$X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \end{pmatrix},\quad y = (10,\ 20,\ 30)$$

Virtually $Y = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 20 & 30 \\ 10 & 20 & 30 \end{pmatrix}$, so

$$X + y = \begin{pmatrix} 11 & 22 & 33 \\ 14 & 25 & 36 \end{pmatrix}.$$

math.title: General broadcasting compatibility rule
math.latex: \text{shape}(A) = (a, b, \dots, n, n{+}1, \dots, m), \quad \text{shape}(B) = (n, n{+}1, \dots, m) \;\Rightarrow\; A \circ B \text{ is defined, broadcasting over axes } a,\dots,n{-}1
math.source_text: one tensor has shape (a, b, … n, n + 1, … m) and the other has shape (n, n + 1, … m). The broadcasting will then automatically happen for axes a through n - 1.

variables.meaning: The smaller tensor; its shape equals the trailing axes of A's shape.
The leading axes of A that B lacks; B is virtually repeated along these.

math.operations: Compare shapes from the right; if B's shape is a suffix of A's shape, prepend size-1 axes to B and repeat along them.
math.purpose: Gives a one-line test for whether an element-wise operation between two differently shaped tensors is legal.
math.interpretation: The smaller tensor is 'applied per slice' of the larger tensor over its leading axes.
math.intuition: The trailing axes must line up exactly; whatever is left over in front is where the copying happens.
math.numerical_example: `(64, 28, 28, 3)` with `(3,)`: suffix matches, broadcasting over the three leading axes — valid. `(32, 10)` with `(32,)`: trailing `10 ≠ 32` — not valid (you would need `(32, 1)`).

code.title: Create a (32, 10) matrix and a (10,) vector
code.original_code:
import numpy as np
X = np.random.random((32, 10))
y = np.random.random((10,))
code.what_it_does: Builds the two operands of the running example: a random rank-2 tensor `X` of shape `(32, 10)` and a random rank-1 tensor `y` of shape `(10,)`.

line_explanations.explanation: Import NumPy under its conventional alias.
`np.random.random((32, 10))` draws 320 uniform numbers in [0, 1) arranged as 32 rows of 10 — callout: 'X is a random matrix with shape (32, 10)'.
`np.random.random((10,))` draws a vector of 10 numbers — callout: 'y is a random vector with shape (10,)'. Note the one-element tuple `(10,)`.

code.inputs_outputs: No inputs; produces `X` (float64, shape (32, 10)) and `y` (float64, shape (10,)).
code.algorithm: Uniform random sampling; the values are irrelevant, only the shapes matter.
code.theory_link: Models a batch of 32 samples with 10 features and a per-feature vector — the same shapes as a layer output and its bias.

parameters.role: Shape tuple for a vector with 10 entries.

pitfalls: Writing `np.random.random(10)` also works, but `np.random.random((10))` is the same as `(10)`, an integer — the trailing comma is what makes a tuple.

code.title: Step 1 — add an empty first axis
code.what_it_does: Inserts a new axis of length 1 at position 0, turning `y` from shape `(10,)` into `(1, 10)` so that its rank matches `X`.

line_explanations.explanation: `axis=0` means the new axis is the first one. Callout: 'The shape of y is now (1, 10)'. The 10 values are unchanged.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: `y` of shape (10,). Output: `y` of shape (1, 10).
code.algorithm: A metadata change only — NumPy returns a view with an extra axis; no data is copied.
code.theory_link: This is the first bullet of the broadcasting definition (p.54): add broadcast axes to match `ndim`.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.role: Position at which to insert the new axis; 0 = leading.

pitfalls: `y[np.newaxis, :]` and `y.reshape(1, 10)` produce the same result; `axis=1` would give a column `(10, 1)`, which broadcasts differently.

code.title: Step 2 — repeat y 32 times along the new axis
code.what_it_does: Repeats the `(1, 10)` tensor 32 times along axis 0 and 1 time along axis 1, producing `Y` with shape `(32, 10)` whose every row equals the original `y`.

line_explanations.explanation: The tuple `(32, 1)` is the repeat count per axis. Callout: 'Repeat y 32 times along axis 0 to obtain Y with shape (32, 10)'. Afterwards `Y[i, :] == y` for all `i` in `range(0, 32)`.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: `y` of shape (1, 10). Output: `Y` of shape (32, 10) — a real, materialised copy (320 numbers).
code.algorithm: Explicit copying of the row 32 times.
code.theory_link: This is the second bullet of the broadcasting definition made concrete; the real `X + y` does this *virtually*.

parameters.role: Number of repetitions along axis 0 and axis 1 respectively.

pitfalls: Do not use `np.tile` in production for this purpose — it allocates the full matrix that broadcasting avoids.

code.title: naive_add_matrix_and_vector — the algorithm behind broadcasting
code.what_it_does: Adds a vector `y` to every row of a matrix `x` using explicit Python loops, returning a new matrix. It shows, at the algorithmic level, what NumPy's broadcast addition computes without ever building a repeated copy of `y`.

line_explanations.explanation: Require `x` to be rank 2 — callout: 'x is a rank-2 NumPy tensor'.
Require `y` to be rank 1 — callout: 'y is a NumPy vector'.
The number of columns of `x` must equal the length of `y`: this is the trailing-axis compatibility condition of the broadcasting rule.
Copy `x` so the caller's array is not modified in place — callout: 'Avoids overwriting the input tensor'.
Outer loop over rows `i`, inner loop over columns `j`; add `y[j]` to `x[i, j]`. Because the index into `y` is only `j`, the same vector is used for every row — the 'virtual repetition' along axis 0.

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: `x` with shape (n, m), `y` with shape (m,). Output: a new array of shape (n, m) with `out[i, j] = x[i, j] + y[j]`.
code.algorithm: O(n·m) element-wise loop; memory O(n·m) for the copy of `x` plus O(m) for `y` — no O(n·m) copy of `y` is needed.
code.theory_link: Implements $Z_{ij} = X_{ij} + y_j$ (formula m1) and is the mixed-shape analogue of `naive_add` on p.53.

parameters.name: x
parameters.role: Rank-2 input tensor (e.g. a batch of feature vectors).

parameters.name: y
parameters.role: Rank-1 tensor added to every row (e.g. a bias vector).

pitfalls: Pure Python loops are orders of magnitude slower than `x + y` (p.54 timed 2.45 s vs 0.02 s for a similar loop).
Forgetting `x.copy()` would silently mutate the caller's array.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written check that the naive loop matches NumPy's broadcast addition
import numpy as np
X = np.random.random((32, 10))
y = np.random.random((10,))
assert np.allclose(naive_add_matrix_and_vector(X, y), X + y)
print((X + y).shape)   # (32, 10)

deeper.title: Why the repetition can be virtual: zero-stride views
deeper.body: Beyond the book: a NumPy array is described by a data pointer, a shape and a tuple of *strides* (bytes to step per axis). To broadcast `y` of shape `(10,)` to `(32, 10)`, NumPy creates a view with shape `(32, 10)` and strides `(0, 8)`: moving along axis 0 advances the pointer by 0 bytes, so all 32 'rows' alias the same 10 floats. You can see this with `np.broadcast_to(y, (32, 10)).strides` → `(0, 8)`. That is precisely what the authors mean by 'the repetition happens at the algorithmic level rather than at the memory level'.

deeper.title: Step by step through the running example
deeper.body:
1. `X.shape == (32, 10)`, `y.shape == (10,)` — ranks differ (2 vs 1).
2. Compare shapes from the right: `10` vs `10` — match.
3. Add a broadcast axis to `y`: `(1, 10)` — ranks now equal.
4. Virtually repeat along the size-1 axis 32 times: `(32, 10)`.
5. Apply element-wise `+`: `Z[i, j] = X[i, j] + y[j]`.

The naive function does steps 2–5 explicitly: the assert on `x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]` is step 2, and indexing `y[j]` inside the `i` loop is steps 3–4.

deeper.title: The bias in a Dense layer
deeper.body: On p.52 a `Dense` layer was written as `output = relu(dot(input, W) + b)`. If `input` is a batch of shape `(32, 784)` and `W` is `(784, 10)`, then `dot(input, W)` is `(32, 10)` and `b` is `(10,)` — exactly this page's shapes. The `+ b` is a broadcast addition: every one of the 32 samples receives the same 10 bias values. The authors imply this motivation on p.54 ('in the Dense layer introduced earlier, we added a rank-2 tensor with a vector').

deeper.title: A stencil on a stack of forms
deeper.body: Imagine 32 identical paper forms (the rows of `X`) and a single transparent stencil with 10 corrections written on it (`y`). You do not photocopy the stencil 32 times; you lay the same stencil over each form in turn and apply the corrections. The stencil is 'repeated' in effect but exists only once — that is virtual broadcasting.

visualizations.title: Broadcasting (32, 10) + (10,)
visualizations.why: The page's running example: see how the (10,) vector is virtually repeated 32 times along a new leading axis to match X.

misconceptions.claim: NumPy builds the enlarged (32, 10) copy of y when you write X + y.
misconceptions.correction: It does not. The page stresses that the repetition is entirely virtual; np.tile is used only to make the mental model concrete.

misconceptions.claim: Any two tensors can be broadcast together.
misconceptions.correction: Only when the smaller shape matches the trailing axes of the larger one (the (n, n + 1, … m) rule). (32, 10) + (32,) fails.

misconceptions.claim: expand_dims changes the data in y.
misconceptions.correction: It only adds an axis of length 1; the 10 values are untouched and no copy is made.

misconceptions.claim: The naive loop and NumPy's broadcast give different results.
misconceptions.correction: They compute the same Z[i, j] = X[i, j] + y[j]; they differ only in speed and memory.

takeaways: Broadcasting = (1) add size-1 axes to the smaller tensor so ranks match, (2) repeat it along those axes to match the larger shape.
Explicitly: np.expand_dims(y, axis=0) takes (10,) to (1, 10); np.tile(y, (32, 1)) takes (1, 10) to (32, 10).
In a real implementation the repetition is virtual — no (32, 10) copy of y is ever stored.
The naive loop x[i, j] += y[j] shows the algorithm: the vector index depends only on the column, so every row gets the same vector.
Rule: shapes (a, b, … n, n + 1, … m) and (n, n + 1, … m) are compatible; broadcasting happens over axes a through n − 1.

questions.question: After `y = np.expand_dims(y, axis=0)` on a vector `y` of shape (10,), what is `y.shape`?
questions.explanation: `axis=0` inserts a new leading axis of size 1, giving (1, 10) as the page states. (10, 1) would require axis=1; (10,) is the original shape; (32, 10) is only reached after tiling.

questions.question: What does the tuple `(32, 1)` mean in `Y = np.tile(y, (32, 1))`?
questions.answer: Repeat y 32 times along axis 0 and once along axis 1, producing Y of shape (32, 10) with every row equal to y.
questions.explanation: np.tile takes a per-axis repetition count; 32 copies stacked along the first axis and no extra copies along the second yield (32, 10), and Y[i, :] == y for all i.

questions.question: The page says the repetition in broadcasting is 'entirely virtual'. What does that mean and why does it matter?
questions.answer: No new rank-2 tensor holding 32 copies of y is allocated; the operation simply reuses y[j] for every row i. This avoids wasting memory and time, which would be 'terribly inefficient' for large batches.
questions.explanation: The authors contrast the algorithmic level (where y is conceptually repeated) with the memory level (where it is not). The naive loop demonstrates the algorithm: indexing y[j] inside the row loop achieves the repetition without storage.

questions.question: According to the general rule on this page, which pair of shapes is compatible for a broadcast element-wise operation?
questions.explanation: The smaller shape must equal the trailing axes of the larger: (3,) matches the last axis of (64, 28, 28, 3), so broadcasting happens over the first three axes. (32,) does not match the trailing 10 of (32, 10); (10, 32) is a prefix, not a suffix, of (10, 32, 3); (5, 4) and (4, 5) have the same rank but mismatched trailing axes.

questions.question: Let X = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] and y = [10, 20, 30]. Compute X + y using the broadcasting rule Z_ij = X_ij + y_j.
questions.explanation: Each row of X receives the same vector y: row 0 becomes (1+10, 2+20, 3+30) and row 1 becomes (4+10, 5+20, 6+30). The index into y depends only on the column j.

questions.question: Why does `naive_add_matrix_and_vector` call `x = x.copy()` before the loops?
questions.answer: To avoid overwriting the input tensor; the function modifies x in place inside the loops, so without the copy the caller's array would be mutated.
questions.explanation: The printed callout says 'Avoids overwriting the input tensor'. The in-place `x[i, j] += y[j]` would otherwise change the array passed in.

questions.question: Without looking, write down the two steps of broadcasting and give the shapes y passes through in the (32, 10) + (10,) example. Then explain in one sentence why NumPy does not actually perform step 2 in memory.
questions.answer: Step 1: add broadcast axes to match ndim — (10,) → (1, 10). Step 2: repeat along the new axes — (1, 10) → (32, 10). NumPy skips the physical copy because the same y[j] can be read for every row, making a materialised copy wasteful.
